murray.about: Andrew Murray (1828–1917), a South African pastor of Scottish descent who served in the Dutch Reformed Church at Wellington near Cape Town, published this book in 1885. It became one of the best-loved Christian works on prayer. Each of its thirty-one lessons opens with a word of Yeshua about prayer, from “Lord, teach us to pray” to His high-priestly prayer, and closes with a prayer of its own. Murray’s great themes are believing prayer, abiding in Messiah (John 15), and intercession as the highest calling of His followers, modelled on Messiah who “always lives to intercede.” A later note on George Müller shows the lessons lived out. Murray wrote as a nineteenth-century churchman and rarely speaks of Israel; the Messianic Filter can render his terms in Hebraic form.
murray.translation: Written in English; the text of the 1885 edition.

enoch.about: 1 Enoch is a Jewish apocalyptic work ascribed to Enoch, who “walked with God” (Genesis 5:24). It is a collection of five books written between about 300 BCE and the turn of the era: the Book of the Watchers (1–36), the Parables (37–71), the Astronomical Book (72–82), the Dream Visions (83–90) and the Epistle of Enoch (91–108). Aramaic fragments of every part but the Parables were found at Qumran. The whole survives only in Ge’ez, and only the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches count it as Scripture. Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, and Peter’s imprisoned spirits and sinning angels echo the Watchers. The Parables’ “Son of Man,” the Elect One who judges, is vital background to Yeshua’s favourite title for Himself.
enoch.translation: R. H. Charles (1917), from the Ethiopic, checked against the Greek and Aramaic witnesses known then. His brackets mark interpolations and restorations; a few passages follow his rearranged order.

1maccabees.about: 1 Maccabees tells the story of the Maccabean revolt, from the decrees of Antiochus IV that defiled the Temple and forbade circumcision, Shabbat and the Torah (167 BCE), through the uprising of the priest Mattathias and his sons, the rededication of the altar by Judah Maccabee, and the rule of his brothers Jonathan and Simon, to the death of Simon in 134 BCE. Written by an unknown Jewish author in the Land of Israel, probably around 100 BCE, it was composed in Hebrew but survives in Greek. It is a sober history in the style of Samuel and Kings and the main source for the rise of the Hasmonean dynasty and the first Chanukah (4:36–59). It belongs to the Septuagint, but not to the Tanakh.
1maccabees.translation: King James Version (1611), from the Greek of the Septuagint; Apocrypha text of the Cambridge Paragraph Bible.

2maccabees.about: 2 Maccabees tells of the Temple’s desecration under Antiochus IV and its recovery by Judah Maccabee, from about 180 to 161 BCE. An anonymous Jewish author wrote it in Greek as a summary of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene, probably in the later second century BCE; the letters at its opening, dated 124 BCE, urge the Jews of Egypt to keep the feast of the Temple’s purification, Chanukah. Its accounts of Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons (chapters 6–7), with their hope of resurrection, lie behind Hebrews 11:35. It is part of the Septuagint, deuterocanonical for Catholic and Orthodox churches and among the Apocrypha for Protestants, but not in the Tanakh. It is the background to the Feast of Dedication that Yeshua kept in Jerusalem (John 10:22).
2maccabees.translation: King James Version (1611), from the Greek of the Septuagint; Apocrypha text of the Cambridge Paragraph Bible.

avot.about: Pirkei Avot, “Chapters of the Fathers” or Ethics of the Fathers, is the one tractate of the Mishnah without law. It opens with the chain of tradition from Moses at Sinai through Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Men of the Great Assembly, then gathers the sayings of the sages down to the generation of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, who edited the Mishnah about 200 CE. Its first chapters bring us the teachers of the Second Temple era: Hillel and Shammai, and Rabban Gamaliel, in whose school Shaul was trained (Acts 22:3). Many sayings sound much like Yeshua’s own teaching. The sixth chapter, on acquiring Torah, was added later for reading. It is traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons between Pesach and Shavuot.
avot.translation: Dr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (Conservative Yeshiva), a close modern translation with supplied words in brackets; CC BY. Hebrew: Romm, Vilna 1913.

mishnah.about: The Mishnah is the first great written collection of the Oral Torah, edited by Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi in the Land of Israel about 200 CE. In Mishnaic Hebrew it records the rulings and debates of the sages, the Tannaim, in six orders: Zeraim (blessings and agriculture), Moed (Shabbat and the festivals), Nashim (marriage), Nezikin (civil law), Kodashim (the Temple service) and Tahorot (purity), in 63 tractates. It became the foundation of both Talmuds. Most of it was set down generations after Yeshua, so it must be read with care as evidence for His day, yet it preserves much of the world of the Gospels: the Temple and its courts, the festivals, the washing of hands, Shabbat, prayer and the debates of Hillel and Shammai.
mishnah.translation: Dr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (Conservative Yeshiva), a close modern translation with supplied words in brackets; CC BY. Hebrew: Romm, Vilna 1913.

1clement.about: First Clement is a letter from the assembly of God in Rome to the assembly in Corinth, where younger members had removed their elders. It names no author, but early tradition gives it to Clement, an elder of Rome, and it is usually dated about 96 CE, though some place it earlier. It is the oldest Christian writing outside the New Testament. Clement calls for humility, repentance and good order, and he does so almost entirely from Israel’s Scriptures: Abraham “our father,” Moses, Rahab, David, and the order of priests and Levites. He tells of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul (chapter 5) and closes with a great intercessory prayer (59–61). Some churches read it in worship, and Codex Alexandrinus bound it with the New Testament.
1clement.translation: Roberts and Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (1885), a careful, literal Victorian rendering from the Greek. The chapter titles are the editors’.

odes.about: The Odes of Solomon are forty-two hymns from the earliest generations of Messiah’s followers, probably written in Syria around 100 CE, in Syriac or Greek. They carry Solomon’s name but do not claim to be his work. Lost for centuries, they were found in 1909 by J. Rendel Harris in a Syriac manuscript; one Ode survives in Greek and five are quoted in Coptic. Full of joy, light, living water and union with the Beloved, they sound close to the Gospel of John and to the thanksgiving hymns of Qumran. Scholars have read them as Jewish-Christian, and they are sometimes called the earliest Christian hymnbook. Several speak in the voice of Messiah Himself.
odes.translation: To come: J. Rendel Harris, from the Syriac (1909; revised with Alphonse Mingana 1916–1920). Not yet added; the track passes over it for now.

hermas.about: The Shepherd of Hermas was written in Rome by Hermas, a former slave, between the late first century and about 150 CE; the Muratorian fragment calls him the brother of Pius, bishop of Rome. It has three parts: five Visions, in which an aged woman who is the assembly shows him a tower being built of living stones; twelve Commandments, or Mandates; and ten Similitudes, or parables, given by the angel of repentance in the form of a shepherd. Its great theme is repentance and a second chance after immersion. It was one of the most widely read books of the early assemblies: Irenaeus quotes it as Scripture and Codex Sinaiticus includes it, though in the end it was not received into the canon.
hermas.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (1885), from the Greek and, for the ending lost in Greek, the Latin.

polycarp.about: Polycarp (about 69–155 CE) was the elder, or bishop, of Smyrna. Irenaeus, who knew him as a boy, says he had been taught by the apostle John. He wrote this letter to the assembly at Philippi, which had asked him for the letters of Ignatius; many date it about 110, soon after Ignatius passed through on his way to martyrdom in Rome; others think it joins a short early note (chapters 13–14) to a later letter. Full of quotations from 1 Peter and Paul, it urges righteousness, warns against the love of money (the elder Valens had fallen into it) and against denying that Messiah came in the flesh. Polycarp was burned at Smyrna in old age for refusing to deny Him.
polycarp.translation: Roberts and Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (1885), from the Greek; chapters 10–12 and 14 survive only in an old Latin version.

didache.about: The Didache, “The Teaching of the Lord through the Twelve Apostles to the Nations,” is an anonymous handbook for assemblies of Gentile believers, probably compiled in Syria in the late first century. Known only by name for centuries, it was found by Philotheos Bryennios in a Constantinople manuscript in 1873. It opens with the Two Ways, of life and of death, close to Jewish ethical teaching, then gives instructions for immersion in living water, fasting, praying the Lord’s Prayer three times a day, and the thanksgiving over cup and bread in the pattern of Jewish blessings. It ends with guidance on apostles and prophets and a watchful hope for the Lord’s coming. It is among the most Jewish of the early writings.
didache.translation: Roberts and Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7 (1886), from the Greek of the Jerusalem manuscript.
